ref.title: Update on cannabis in human sexuality

sources.title: Update on cannabis in human sexuality
money: Open access funding provided by Bar-Ilan University.

design.quote: This review aims to provide an overview of the current literature on the effects of cannabis on several sexual functions, including sexual desire, arousal, orgasm, and sexual satisfaction.
design.text: Review paper on cannabis effects on human sexuality

findings.where: General effects of cannabis on sexuality in humans
findings.quote: Cannabis, widely believed to enhance sexual desire, has been found to have a bidirectional effect on sexual functioning. On the one hand, cannabis use has been associated with positive outcomes, such as prolonged intercourse, improved orgasm quality, and increased sexual satisfaction in both men and women; conversely, cannabis use has been linked to negative effects, including erectile dysfunction, sterility, and reduced testosterone levels.
findings.text: Cannabis use can improve sexual desire, prolong intercourse, improve orgasm quality, and increase sexual satisfaction in both men and women, but it can also cause erectile dysfunction, sterility, and reduced testosterone levels.

findings.where: Effects of dose and frequency › Dosage
findings.quote: In a review of recent studies, Kipping and Lynn found that moderate doses of cannabis improved female sexual function in domains such as orgasm, libido, and arousal. However, they also noted that high doses of cannabis may have negative effects on female sexual function.
findings.text: Moderate doses of cannabis improve female sexual function in orgasm, libido, and arousal, whereas high doses may have negative effects on female sexual function.
findings.second_hand: In a review of recent studies, Kipping and Lynn found that moderate doses of cannabis improved female sexual function in domains such as orgasm, libido, and arousal.

findings.quote: Reports suggest that cannabis has the potential to enhance sexual pleasure, reduce inhibitions, alleviate anxiety and shame, and promote intimacy and connection with sexual partners (Parent et al.). Furthermore, it has been associated with increased pleasure during masturbation and enhanced sensory experiences during sexual encounters (Moser et al.).
findings.text: Cannabis may enhance sexual pleasure, reduce inhibitions, alleviate anxiety and shame, promote intimacy, increase pleasure during masturbation, and enhance sensory experiences during sexual encounters.
findings.second_hand: Reports suggest that cannabis has the potential to enhance sexual pleasure, reduce inhibitions, alleviate anxiety and shame, and promote intimacy and connection with sexual partner

limits.quote: Studies investigating the impact of cannabis use frequency on human sexuality have yielded diverse and occasionally conflicting findings, necessitating additional research with a focus on controlling for more covariates.
limits.text: The impact of cannabis use frequency on human sexuality is unclear due to diverse and conflicting findings, requiring further research with better control of covariates.

money: No funding was used to conduct this study.

findings.quote: Results from this study indicated that both men and women see benefits from using cannabis before sexual intercourse or masturbation.
findings.text: People who use cannabis before sex report benefits to sexual functioning and satisfaction.

findings.quote: the forms of wax and flower predicted increased sexual functioning and satisfaction.
findings.text: People who use wax or flower forms of cannabis report increased sexual functioning and satisfaction.

findings.quote: Women may be more likely to orgasm when using cannabis before sexual encounters, which could contribute to equity in the amount of sexual pleasure and satisfaction experienced by both women and men.
findings.text: Women who use cannabis before sex may experience higher orgasm rates, potentially reducing the orgasm inequality gap.

limits.quote: Data were collected using the online survey tool “Qualtrics” from a self-selected, convenience sample of adults over the age of 18 who reported previous cannabis use.
